translations.text: A discourse delivered by Apa John, archbishop of Constantinople, on repentance and self-control.
The blessed Paul, the apostle to the Gentiles, who became a teacher of the church, who strove to equal the bodiless powers in his way of life,
who finished the race and kept the faith,
who shone through fasting, hunger, thirst, and dangers,
who persevered on the road from Jerusalem all the way to Illyricum, preaching the gospel:
this angel who belongs to earth,
and this man who belongs to heaven,
the one who has Christ speaking within him,
the dwelling place of the Holy Spirit,
The one who was caught up to the third heaven and heard mysterious words.
the one who was taken to paradise,
the one whose love and zeal for Christ cannot be expressed,
the caretaker of the churches,
the spokesman for godliness,
the bridal escort of those who have believed in Christ,
the herald and teacher of the Gentiles,
the one who showed us the way to ascend to heaven,
said, “I discipline my body.
I make it a slave,
so that, after preaching to others, I myself may not be rejected.”
If, then, this holy man, who possesses so many virtues, who said boldly, “I am not aware of anything wrong that I have done,”
was afraid and spoke in this way,
then what will we do, we miserable people who have achieved no virtue?
Should we not, then, keep watch and pray at all times, and ask God not for gold or silver or any of this world’s wealth, but only for the wealth of heaven,
and rejoice in the Lord?
Some people, indeed, rejoice in wealth.
Others, however, over drinking places and meals;
and others over worldly beauty and glory.
But let the virgin herself rejoice in the Lord.
And let her seek the honor that comes from him, saying, “My honor is before you.”
There is nothing as ugly or contemptible as a soul filled with passion.
For this reason, we ought to take care of our soul
at all times and say, like Saint David, “Lord, give strength to my beauty,”
so that when the bridegroom sees the soul’s beauty, he will say, “You are altogether beautiful, my companion, and there is no blemish in you.”
But even if you succeed in virtue, be careful not to become proud of your beauty,
lest God turn his face away from you because of your pride.
For what can you do that is worthy of what he endured for you?
He humbled himself for your sake; he gave his precious, holy blood for you.
He who feeds every living creature fasted in the flesh for your sake.
He who created the sweetness of honey
tasted bitterness for your sake.
He who adorns heaven with the choir of stars
wore a crown of thorns for your sake.
Having become obedient even to the point of death.
And death on a cross.
Therefore, we should not boast about these things,
but repent and weep and listen to the one who says, “Be grieved over what you say in your hearts on your beds,”
so that we may remember at night the things we did during the day and sigh over them.
This is what Ahab did when he was grieved.
He fasted and clothed himself in sackcloth.
And what did the Lord say about him? “I will not bring disaster upon him during his lifetime.”
For this very reason, the Savior pronounced those who weep blessed.
Those who do not weep over an injury or the loss of money.
but over their sins.
You too should say, like David, “I will wash my bed every night.
I will soak my couch with my tears.” And again, “My eyes poured out streams of water because they did not keep your law.” Wash away the stain with tears.
Beat your breast.
Bring to mind your sins
that you committed.
Traps were once laid for you through your eyes.
You once opened your windows to evil.
You harmed your soul through your eyes.
The eyes that looked at evil—
heal them now with tears.
And close your windows so that you do not look at worthless things again,
lest you fall into a bad habit.
For habit drags whoever follows it into great sins.
You are wearing a splendid garment. Take care not to sit down just anywhere, lest it become stained.
For if you disregard the first stain, the second, and the third, then, since the whole garment has become stained,
you no longer hesitate to sit down anywhere dirty.
What, then, shall we do? What is needed now is powerful prayer,
lest you strike your foot against a stone,
and so that the angel of the Lord may surround you and rescue you, and you too may be able to say, “The angel who rescues me from every evil.”
And so that the angel may call to you too from heaven, as he did to Abraham.
For the angels love those who love their own Lord.
He said, “Take up a psalm and sound a tambourine,
a sweet-sounding harp with a lyre.”
You take one; three are demanded of you.
For we are made up of three parts, as the apostle says: “May he keep your spirit whole, along with your soul and your body.”
The psaltery is the spirit.
The lyre is the soul.
As for the tambourine, what covers it is a dead skin.
Put the flesh to death, then,
so that you can bless the Lord with a tambourine and a dance.
For the Lord himself burned the flesh for your sake.
Take care that he does not say to you, “What profit is there in my blood?”
What, then, can you give in return to the one who endured all these sufferings for your sake?
Become a fruit-bearing tree, so that the Lord’s blessing may be upon you.
Bear fruit according to your ability.
If you cannot produce a hundred, which is the full amount, at least produce sixty, which is half.
If this is difficult for you, at least give thirty, which is one third.
Only act according to your ability,
lest you become fruitless, and they cut you down and throw you into the fire.
If you will not become a vessel of gold or silver, do not become wood, grass, or straw either, for these are fuel for the fire.
Do not do the deeds that God hates, lest they stand against you on the day of judgment like an image,
Then you will begin to confess them in that place, without a witness.
without an accuser, without proof,
when you see everything you have done,
and everything you have said heedlessly, pictured before your eyes.
Weep before the time comes, lest you hear in that place, “This is not the time for repentance.”
For there is no repentance in this place.
As long as we have time, let us work.
If the time slips from our hands,
there is no way for us to find another opportunity.
For this reason, then, blessed Paul teaches us, saying, “As long as we have time, let us do what is good.”
And again: “Look, now is the acceptable time.”
Let us weep over the deeds we have done wickedly.
Let our tears flow down our cheeks. Let us beat our breasts,
so that we may escape the weeping and gnashing of teeth in the place where we are going.
Let us also weep like David,
so that we may be called blessed. He did not merely weep casually like this,
but soaked his bed with his tears, being a watchful tree.
It was on a single night that he sinned.
He, in turn, wept night after night throughout his whole life, without fail, confessing these words
of this kind before God: “Lord, forgive me, because you gave me my eyes so that I might see the light with them,
but I used them to look wickedly.
Since, then, I went astray through my eyes,
I therefore wipe away my sins through tears.”
Let us leave our evil habits behind and move up to the city in heaven.
Let us discipline our body and make it a slave, so that we do not make our soul a slave of the devil.
Let meditation on the words of God burn up the pleasures that dwell within us,
which are like wild beasts.
As we always carry the death of our Lord Jesus Christ in our body.
Let us remember the one who said, “Be sober and keep watch.”
Let no one receive a crown while sleeping.
Let no one receive prizes while being forgetful and snoring.
Rather, the one who endures many wounds and blows is the one who will receive honor from the judge of the contest.
The enemy flees from the one who is sober, but plunders the one who is sleeping.
Therefore, you have understood that you have wicked enemies.
Do not give sleep to your eyes,
or slumber to your eyelids,
so that you may escape like a gazelle from a trap and like a bird from a snare.
Let us always flee from the worries of this life and its snares.
Since we have renounced the world, let us not concern ourselves again with worldly things.
For the deceiver’s traps are many.
He said, “Your adversary, the devil, walks around roaring like a lion, seeking not merely to seize possessions,
but to devour your souls.”
Flee from the deceiver’s cunning,
and say, “Through you I will escape from a den of robbers,
and through my God I will leap over a wall.”
Do not refuse suffering, lest you refuse the crown.
The merchant does not make a profit without enduring waves to obtain wealth.
The athlete who competes endures blows, looking forward to the crown.
The farmer does not find fruit unless he first sows the seeds through his own hard work.
This is how those who look forward to the kingdom of heaven regard afflictions as nothing, taking courage from the hope of the good things to come.
Therefore, let us pay attention and always keep watch, for our bridegroom will appear to them from the bridal chamber.
So that when we hear his voice, we will rise and meet him, ready.
For he said, “Let your waists be girded and your lamps burning, and be like people waiting for their master.”
Look, even now the Savior calls the vigilant person blessed, saying, “Blessed is that servant whose master comes and finds him keeping watch.”
Just as he calls those who keep watch blessed,

so he considers the careless person miserable, saying, “If that wicked servant says in his heart, ‘My master will be delayed,’ and begins to beat his fellow servants and to eat and drink with drunkards,
that servant’s master will come on a day he does not know and at an hour he does not expect, and will cut him in two and assign him his portion with the unbelievers.”
If the one who says, “My master will be delayed,” will be cut in two, then what will they do to the one who does not look forward to him at all?
Therefore, my dear friends, we ought to be found ready at every moment for this single [?], which comes only once.
For there is no way for us to return again and put right what we have neglected.
Therefore, let us be ready at every moment, so that we may say confidently, “God, my heart is ready; my heart is ready.”
We are in a great war in this life.
The sinners, who are the demons, have prepared their bow.
One shoots arrows into our ears so that we will listen to slander with pleasure.
Another shoots at our eyes to make us look wickedly at things that are improper.
Another shoots at our tongue to make us insult our brother.
And another shoots at our bellies, stirring us to gluttony.
Another shoots at our hands, drawing us into robbery and excessive greed.
Yet another moves our feet to make them walk toward evil.
Because of all these things, the blessed Paul strengthens us.
He wrote, “Take up God's full armor and the helmet of the Spirit,
with which you will be able to extinguish every flaming arrow of the evil one.”
Let us listen to the voice of the prophet who says, “You have been told, human being, what is good,
and what the Lord requires of you, except to practice justice and righteousness,
to love mercy, and to be ready to follow the Lord your God.”
Therefore, let us forget what is behind and stretch forward toward what is ahead.
Let us nourish ourselves in the Lord and delight in his words.
Let us not be idle, standing about like this aimlessly and in vain. Rather, since we have our Lord, let us serve him in truth.
Look at his great love for humanity toward us: sometimes he encourages us,
and at other times he threatens us with punishments.
At other times he teaches us obedience, promising a reward to those who will obey him.
Therefore, having girded the loins of our heart with truth,
let us serve the good Lord, our Savior.
Let us remember everything he underwent for our sake.
He was born as a human being for our sake.
He was brought up as a human being; he was young in age.
He was baptized for our sake.
He went hungry, he slept, and he became thirsty for our sake.
He suffered sorrow, and they plotted against him.
They whipped him and insulted him.
Finally, they handed him over to death for our sake.
Let us therefore always remember the one who endured all these things for our sins.
“You have not yet reached the point of shedding blood,” he said.
“But you are struggling against sin.” This means that we are not now being required to give our blood for Christ.
Rather, a life free from sin is being sought from us.
Remember also our Savior’s acts of healing: he healed the sick.
He cast out demons and made the lame walk.
He made the blind see, along with all the other things that we are not in a position to recount one by one.
As the culmination of all these things, he graciously gave us the way to ascend to heaven, so that we too might follow him through a life of virtue and gain our citizenship in heaven.
In keeping with the dignity of the place where our name has been written.
Scripture has called us strangers and foreigners so that we might disregard the things of this world.
Pleasure is like a dog.
If you chase it away, it runs off; but if you feed it, it stays with you.
For this reason James said, “Stand against the devil, and he will flee from you.”
Let us not think that it is possible for us to repent in Hades.
For the medicine of repentance has no power in that place.
But even if we gnash our teeth and our tongue burns, there is no one who will dip his finger in water for us in that place.
Instead, we too will hear the words that this rich man heard.
Since we have therefore realized, my beloved, that the affairs of this world are not worth even dreams, and that we are staying in an inn from which we must certainly depart,
let us give thought to the journey and the provisions that we will take with us on the road.
As we depart from this life, let us put on the garments that Paul advised us to wear when he said, “Clothe yourselves with heartfelt compassion, kindness, and humility.”
We do not need gold in that place; rather, it is a drop of water that we need.
We do not need leaves, but fruit. We do not need words, but deeds.
For he said, “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does the will of my Father who is in heaven.”
So let us not deceive ourselves.
Even if someone spends his entire life eating and drinking, it is nothing compared with the endless ages.
For here, both good things and bad things have their end.
But in that place there are good things that last forever and punishments without end.
Here, even if the body burns, the soul comes out unharmed.
But in that place, even if the body rises imperishable, the soul is burned continually.
For sinners must rise imperishable, not so that they may receive glory, but so that they may be tormented without ever dying.
If one can indeed endure the air of a furnace when it is not heated beyond what is proper, then what will we do when we are handed over to the river of fire that flows before Christ’s judgment seat?
For everyone must be tested by that fire.
Let us examine the seal to see whether our purse is intact or whether our treasure has been plundered.
For all our deeds are exposed to the one who will call us to account, and there is no way to deceive that judge.
As long as we still have time, come, let us heal the wounds of our soul with tears.

If the prophet Jeremiah wept over the destruction of the temple, which was built of real stones, saying, “Leave me to weep bitterly,” how much more should we weep over our own temple, which is more highly honored,
in which there is not a golden censer, but in which the Holy Trinity dwells.
If, when we see someone who has died, we weep over him out of habit, then who could be so utterly senseless that he would not weep over his own soul, which has died through sin?
Therefore, you should weep not over a corpse, but over the death of your soul.
Remember that the appointed time has drawn near.
And the judge is standing at the door. The night is far advanced; the day has drawn near.
Let no one remain asleep when the night passes and the sun rises.
Let us therefore rise from the slumber of dreams. Let us bear fruit worthy of repentance, as it is written.
Repentance does not take a long time, and many of the martyrs received the crown in a short moment.
Even if we have committed sins that lead to death, let us not give up on ourselves. For we have remedies that bring salvation: tears.
For making a mistake in something is part of human nature.
But persisting in the mistake is the work of Satan.
For falling is not the evil; rather, failing to rise from the fall is the evil and the ruin.
Therefore our Lord cried out to us through the prophet, “Is there no balm in Gilead?
Or is there no physician in that place?
Why, then, has healing not come to the daughter of my people?”
Now, if a part of our body becomes sick, we seek out physicians and make every effort until we heal the sick part of our body.
But when our soul is sick, we neglect it and take no care at all for its salvation.
Let us fear the one who has the power to destroy our soul and our body in Gehenna.
Come, let us run to the ocean of God's mercies before the time of torment.
And let us too say with Saint David, “You will wash me with it, and I will become whiter than snow.”
The good shepherd stands ready, wanting to snatch our souls from the lion's mouth before it swallows them.
He cries out to us too, “My son, you have sinned; do not keep doing it.”
And, “Does someone fall and not get up?”
“Or does someone turn away and not turn back again?”
And, “Return to me, children who have strayed, and I will heal your failings.”
The one who said this does not lie [?]: “I did not come to judge the world, but so that the world might be saved through me.”
Only let us repent.
“For I do not desire the sinner's death,” he said, “but rather that the sinner turn away from his evil way and live.”
None of those who love bodies, even if he burns with passion for the woman he loves, can love her so completely
as God loves the soul that will repent.
And he invited the woman who had prostituted herself many times, saying, “And after she had prostituted herself in all these ways, I said to her, ‘Return to me.’”
For such is God's love for humanity:
he never turns away from anyone who approaches him in repentance,
even if that person has fallen into the pit of evil. Instead, he stretches out his hand to him, saying, “Return to me, and I will redeem you.”
And again, “Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts.”
For if a physician—even if the sick person becomes discouraged and insults him—
[?] the physician despises him. Nor does he retaliate against him for the insults; instead, he gives him medicine with kindness.
How much more will the good God, the true physician of our souls!
Only let us not neglect our own salvation.
For often a wrestler falls in the contest, but in the end he gets up and receives a crown.
And a soldier, after being wounded and treated, fights again and wins greater distinction than those who were never struck at all.
And how many merchants, after their ship sinks and they lose their cargo, do not give up!
Instead, they return to trading again and become rich.
For was the fire of Gehenna prepared for us? No, it was prepared for the devil and his angels.
Only let us not kindle that fire for ourselves and then hear in turn, “Go into the flame that you have kindled.”
There is no disease that is incurable with the medicine of the physician of our souls.
But perhaps you will say, “I cannot reach perfection.”
If you cannot reach perfection, if you cannot be like the sun, at least be like the stars.
Only move from the earth up to heaven, and become like the stars that shine.
It is better for you to do a few good deeds than to do nothing at all.
You have been told about giving a cup of cold water and visiting the sick and those in prison.
For if we are to be punished for our words and our thoughts,
how much more will he reward us for our good deeds, even if they are small!
So let us endure hardship for a little while, so that we may not be left behind when it comes to eternal life.
For if it were possible for us to die many times, we ought to do this until we see Christ coming in his glory.
We will not see him through a riddle, but will behold him as he is, with our own eyes, according to the testimony of the apostle John, who speaks about God.
If, when we see the beauty of a body here, we marvel at it,
even though the beauty of bodies comes from fluids and phlegm, and after death they become worms, ashes, and dust,
how much more will we marvel when we behold that beauty which is imperishable, unfading, and undefiled!
Peter saw only a very faint glimmer of his glory.
He said to us, “It is good for us to stay here.”
What, then, will happen to us when we behold all that glory?

If we call those close to the king here fortunate when we see him coming out on a golden chariot, wearing his crown and purple robe, then how much more fortunate will we be when we are placed at the right hand of the king of all, the judge of everyone!

If you had been promised a kingdom, but the road to the country where that kingdom lay was difficult and rough, with rocky ground and steep terrain, would you not endure all these things until you obtained that kingdom?
Do not say, “I have already been caught in my sins; I cannot turn back to God.”
Even if the devil has already thrown us down, let us get up quickly.
For our Lord loves humanity.
He will run out to meet us and welcome us to himself, just as he did for the young son who squandered his share of the property.
Let us remember that after Solomon became king and experienced all the splendid things of this life,
he said, “What is in them all is emptiness and emptiness.”

If rulers make every effort to be honored by those sitting in the theaters, even though most of those there are poor, despised people, slaves, and foreigners, then how much more should we strive to be acclaimed in that theater, the place where the angels, the archangels, and all the saints gather!
Do not let the sexually immoral and the tax collectors enter the kingdom before us.
Many remedies and means of help, differing from one another, have been set before us in the Holy Scripture.
Ahab felt sorrow over the sin he had committed and escaped God's wrath through this remedy; Nebuchadnezzar escaped through almsgiving.
The people of Nineveh escaped through this remedy of fasting.
The prostitute appeased God toward herself because of her tears.
The robber became a citizen of paradise through faith.
Having taken up these poultices and these medicines,
let us heal our souls of the wounds of sin that we inflict on ourselves.
Let us too say to the true physician, “Heal me, Lord, and I will be healed,” and, “Heal my soul, for I have sinned against you.”
And the true physician will receive us and say, “I am the one, I am the one who wipes away your sins, and I will remember them.”
You have seen this abundance of medicine and these various remedies, which the physician has mercifully laid out for us to treat the various diseases and wounds.
Choose whichever of these you wish for the healing of your soul.
If you cannot show mercy like Nebuchadnezzar, at least grieve over your sins like Ahab. If you cannot fast like the people of Nineveh,
at least wash away your sins with your tears like the prostitute, and run to the merciful one, saying with David, “Have mercy on me, God, according to your great mercy.”
“It was not a snake that bit me, so that I should run to a snake charmer, nor was I stained with mud, so that I should wash myself with water.
Rather, it was the devil who injected his venom into me, and I was stained with the mud of my lawlessness.
For this reason I need the great mercy of your love for humanity.”
Just turn your attention to him and ask him,
and the Father of mercy will grant you mercy, the one who said, “If the lawless person turns away from his evil way, I will not remember any of the lawless deeds he has done.”
Just reveal your wound to him and say, “Have mercy on me. Have mercy on my body and my soul.
Have mercy on me in this age and the other.
Have mercy on me because of the weakness of my nature and because of the ocean of your goodness.”
Only desire healing, and the physician will take the initiative with his medicines.
For he seeks your salvation. He is the one who brought back the sheep that had gone astray.
He is the one who sent his servant out onto the roads to invite the evil and the good to the wedding.
Look, he offers the kingdom of heaven to you too.
If you cannot buy it with money, buy it for yourself with small pieces of bread. He offers you the kingdom of heaven in exchange for these.
Look, the prophet cries out, saying, “Who is the person who desires life, who loves to see good days?” And, “You who have no money, go and buy for yourselves.”
For what does the seller seek, when we have no money to give?
If not, give the payment for your soul. Offer fasting. Offer tears.
If you have none of these other things, then keep your tongue from evil and your lips from speaking deceit.
This will be the beginning of your soul’s salvation. But pay attention to yourself.
Even if you fast, guard yourself against becoming proud.
Even if you give to those in need, do not do it for praise from people.
Instead, when the day of fasting has passed, examine yourself and see what you have gained for yourself through fasting, lest you be found just as you were before you fasted.
But consider which sins you have left behind, or in what you have made progress.
What good achievement have you gained for yourself?
Or what weakness have you corrected through fasting?
See whether you have withdrawn from anger and left rage behind.
See whether you have stopped insulting people, speaking against your brother, and bearing ill will toward your neighbor.
See whether you have stopped swearing oaths and speaking frivolous words, idle words, or coarse jokes.
See what good you have gained for yourself.
If you have abstained only from bread and other foods, but have not abstained from the passions or acquired virtues for yourself, then what have you gained through fasting?
Do not say, “So-and-so has insulted me; I too will insult him.”
“So-and-so has ruined my reputation.”
“I too will ruin his. So-and-so has treated me unjustly.”
“I too will take my revenge on him.”
Instead, leave room for the true judge, who will repay each person according to their deeds.
For all these things will be exposed and examined in that theater where the whole inhabited world will gather,
in the place where no one will be able to help another and rescue them from the sentence that cannot be appealed,
at that judgment seat. Neither Moses nor Noah nor Daniel nor even Abraham, who loves his children, will be able to save one of his children from punishment.
Let us remember that we are guilty of many sins, both hidden and openly visible.
For he said, “If you pay attention to lawlessness, who will be able to stand?”
And why am I speaking about hidden sins?
If he judges us for those that are openly visible, what forgiveness will there be for us?
If he examines us or questions us about our negligence in our prayers and our faintheartedness,
or because we stand before [?], arranging something or thinking about something,
we do not give him the kind of honor that slaves give their masters, or that soldiers give their commanders, or that friends give their friends.
For when we speak with our companions, you will find that we pay very close attention to them. But when we pray to God about our sins, we do so carelessly.
And you will indeed find that our knees are bent down, while our hearts imagine things and wander among the affairs of the world.
If he questions us about this alone, where will we be able to stand?
And what will we do if he brings forward the accusations we make against one another, along with our jealousies and hatreds?
What will we do if he examines us about our malicious looks and questions us about our evil desires? If he demands an account of our contempt, will we be able to open our mouths?
And if he judges us about our love of human praise, which we have mixed with our prayers, our fasts, and our acts of charity,
will we be able to look up to heaven at all?
If he examines us about the deceit we devise against one another—when our brother is with us, we speak with him as a friend,
but when he is away from us, we accuse him as though he were an enemy.
And if he calls us to account for our false oaths, our lies, our groundless anger against one another, and our envy,
and for the way we grieve when we see one of our companions enjoying a good reputation or receiving more honor than we do, and the way we rejoice over others when some misfortune overtakes them,
how much punishment will we be liable to for things like these?
If he calls us to account for our carelessness in our assemblies—for you will find that our Lord himself speaks with us through the Scriptures,
while we turn away from him and speak with our fellow servants—
how severe a punishment will we be liable to for such conduct?
Therefore, let us keep Gehenna before our eyes at all times.
Even if we had not been threatened with Gehenna at all, we ought to remember our sins at all times. How much more so when it stands ready for us!
Remember the judge, then.
For look, he has told you about the punishment beforehand so that you may escape the danger.
If he commands you to fast, you find an excuse in your weakness.
If he tells you to give alms, you find an excuse in your poverty.
If he tells you not to store things up here, you find an excuse in caring for your children.
If he tells you, “Do not be angry, do not be envious, do not hate, and do not insult your neighbor,” what, then, will you say in response to these things?
Therefore you have no defense, nor will you receive forgiveness for such things. How will you be able to lift your hands toward heaven while these things are in your soul?
But often you will say, “They have treated me unjustly. They have deprived me of my possessions. They have harmed me. They have spoken ill of me.”
Therefore, bear it patiently and wait for the ruler’s verdict.
If a slave insults you, you do not strike him, but you report him to his master.
How much more should you give way to the one who said, “Leave judgment to me; I will repay, says the Lord.”
For you know that you must be brought before a fearsome judgment seat, where neither an advocate nor money will be able to help you.
And that your soul will come out through that river of fire which flows before Christ’s judgment seat.
Send a father ahead of you to that place.
Let the fountain of your tears be in proportion to the sins you have committed.
If your sin is small, then a little weeping is enough.
If your transgression is great, then you also need floods of tears.
But if you are free from sin, lend your tears to your brother and weep with him over his sins.
The place through which sin entered—that is, the eyes—
let healing also come through it.
Let us repent before the door of repentance is shut against us.
Therefore, let the one who says, “I am standing,” take care not to fall.
But let the one who has stumbled and fallen hurry to get up, and do not let him give up on himself.
For it is written, “The Lord raises up those who have fallen.”
A person may be shaken a little, as the holy David said: “As for me, my feet almost slipped; my steps nearly gave way.”
And again: “When I say, ‘My foot has slipped,’ it is your mercy, Lord, that helps me.”
Then again: “They pushed me to make me fall, but the Lord helped me.”
But the one who has fallen also has encouragement not to remain in his downfall. He said, “Does someone who falls not get up?”
But take care that, having heard of the Lord’s goodness, you do not become careless.
It is also written, “God is a just judge, strong and patient.”
He does indeed accept the repentance of those who turn to him, because he loves humanity.
But he said, “If you do not turn back, he will sharpen his sword.”
Listen: he said, “He will sharpen it.”
But he is not striking yet, so that when you see that he has sharpened the sword,
Act before the sentence is pronounced, and let fear awaken you to repentance.
For he said, “He has drawn his bow and made it ready.”
But since you have not yet been made a target, do not despise the judge’s patience.
Listen to the Savior’s patience as he says, “Be reconciled to the one who brings a lawsuit against you.” Your adversary, or the one who fights against you, is with you at all times.
You cannot separate yourself from this one. Paul will show you who he is when he says, “For the flesh desires what is opposed to the spirit, and the spirit what is opposed to the flesh.”
These, then, oppose one another.
The spirit opposes the flesh, wiping away worldly desire through hope in the kingdom of heaven.
The flesh, in turn, opposes the spirit, inclining toward the earth and its pleasures.
Therefore be reconciled with the one who brings a case against you, while he is with you on the road.
For when the journey is over, you will no longer find another opportunity for repentance.

Take care that the one who brings a lawsuit against you does not hand you over to the judge, and the judge hand you over to the officer—that is, the merciless powers in charge of the punishments—and they throw you into prison, which is the outer darkness, until you pay the last penny.
For you will be judged not only for your deeds, but also for your thoughts and your plans.
Since we understand all these things, then, let us help ourselves.
When we experience punishment, then we will understand that pleasure is bitter and that it brings us intense bitterness in return.
Since this is how things stand, my beloved, let us plead with the merciful God not to hand us over to the demons.
Let us too say with Saint David, “Do not hand me over to those who seize me unjustly.”
For they are the ones who now urge us into sin.
They are also the ones who will become our accusers on the day of judgment.
For not only the devil, but all the other demons as well, will accuse us, saying, “Were we not the ones who served you in sexual immorality, anger, the love of empty glory, and slander?”
Let us fear that day, that hour when our own thoughts will become bitter judges against us, and everything we have done will stand against us, portrayed before us like a picture.
Let us plead with our Lord with all our heart.
For although we are clothed in weak flesh, the one who is ready to help us and save us into his kingdom is also great.
We [?] for three reasons: either because of his goodness, or because he loves us too, or because of his beauty.
What other beauty, then, compares with that of our Lord?
As David says, “He is more beautiful than the sons of men.”
Who, then, is a benefactor like him? He has prepared for those who love him the good things that no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and that have never entered the human heart.
Who, then, can love us in this way, as our Lord and our Father does?
He cries out, “Will a mother forget her children?
Or will a bride forget the adornment placed on her?
Or will a virgin forget the sash tied around her? But I will not forget,” says the Lord.
Look at blessed David and the way he longs to see the Lord. He said, “When will I come and appear before my God?”
He did not want to remain until the appointed end of his life. Instead, he burned with longing to leave this place and see the one he loves.
Truly, such love and such eagerness belong to a soul devoted to wisdom, which has taken wing and is flying toward heaven.
You too, love this alone, and pass over all the affairs of this life as though they were shadows.
Remember eternal life at all times,
the everlasting kingdom, dancing with the angels, the glory of immortality, and life with Christ, in which there is no distress. He said, “Distress has fled, along with sorrow and sighing.”
Reflect on this life: there is nothing in it except sorrow, weeping, distress, shame, neglect, sin, suffering, old age, and death.
David, then, was contemplating these things, and things even worse than these: robbery, widowhood, untimely deaths, punishments, and all the other afflictions that prevail in this life.
He longed to be free of all these things.
He said, “When will I come and appear before my God?”
He wanted to depart from this place and go to the place where there are peace, joy, love, splendor, freedom from worry, and all the other good things that no words can describe.
Therefore, you too, since you hope to enjoy such delight, must not be careless.
Instead, let your lamp burn continually, and be ready to meet the bridegroom,
so that you too may hear, “Enter into the joy of your Lord.”
We must keep watch and pray at all times.
For if, even after God said to the devil, “Do not touch my servant Job,”
he continued hoping to bring him down, how much more will he struggle against us, who are in his power,
to bring us down? We need a constant vigil to guard our souls.
For a soldier often keeps vigil during marches, and a fisherman does not sleep, but stays awake all night until he catches a great many fish.
Likewise, a vine grower keeps vigil so that no one damages his vineyard. In the same way, a shepherd keeps vigil, guarding his flock of sheep,
as the patriarch Jacob said, “I was burning in the heat of the day and the frost of the night, and sleep fled from my eyes.”
What is the reason for these nights spent keeping watch like this? “In case,” he said, “a wild animal should kill even one sheep.”
If he takes such great care of an irrational sheep, how much care ought we to take of our rational soul, which is more precious than anything else?
This soul will be made to stand before a terrifying judgment seat to answer for everything it has done.
Therefore, let us cast off the burden of our sins before reaching the place of judgment.
For there is no way for us to repent in that place.
That is why our departure from the body has been appointed but remains hidden from us, so that we may be afraid at all times.
If, in the courtroom here, those appointed to be judged become agitated and stiff with fear whenever they hear the herald’s voice calling out,
how much more will those appointed to stand before the terrifying judgment seat, surrounded by thousands upon thousands and tens of thousands upon tens of thousands of angels!
Look at the blessed Jacob: when he put a stone under his head and went to sleep, he saw a ladder on the ground with its top reaching up to heaven.
And the angels and God were going up and coming down on it.
They carry the prayers up before God and bring us the gifts of grace from him.
All these, then, must watch us.
Rather, they will grieve over us.
If they rejoice when they see us repenting, they likewise grieve over our negligence.
For our conscience always finds fault with us, pricking us over what we have done, especially when we speak about the judgment that is to come.
Nevertheless, rebuke through good words is good.
If only they had rebuked that rich man instead of burning his tongue in a fire that never goes out!
You desire virginity. If you keep the commandments, the Lord will grant it to you.
For if you say in prayer, “Guard me, Lord, like the pupil of an eye,” he in turn will say to you, “Guard my words and my commandments like the pupils of your eyes.”
Whenever you keep his commandments, he in turn will care for your soul, and you will say about yourself, “Whoever touches you is like someone who touches the pupil of his eye.”
Now, then, beloved, you have put your hand to the plow. Do not turn back. Do not become like a pillar of salt.
Let your tongue always speak about the judgment that is to come, so that you may benefit and become an excellent person through fear of that place of judgment.
Do not let anger, sorrow, or any other passion rule over you, causing you to speak out without thinking.
Instead, let the Lord’s law always be in your mouth, so that your eyes may come out [?] through all these things.
And let your words accord with God’s law.
Keep the lawgiver always before your eyes. Let him dwell with you and be your adviser.
Even if you see someone living in luxury and enjoying great wealth, know that he will quickly wither like grass.
Let him delight in food; you, for your part, delight in the words of the Lord.
Many virgins became martyrs. If [?] they conquered death, though they were women,
should you, for your part, as a man, not conquer desire?
Strive to make your limbs motionless, so that you will not only conquer desire,
but also restrain yourself from anger and rage.
Let the tongue have limits.
Take care: do not let your conscience condemn you before the judgment.
Remember that all our deeds must be revealed.
We do not want even one person here to see us behaving shamefully.
Then where will we hide there, among thousands upon thousands and tens of thousands upon tens of thousands?
But because John was a holy virgin, he leaned against Jesus’ chest.
Likewise, let the soul that wishes to become the bride of Jesus Christ preserve its purity, so that the tree will be known by its fruit.
But the righteous person openly professes faith.
Always remember the good confession of Christ, taking into your heart the remembrance of the last day. Guard yourself on every side, especially your tongue.
He said, “The tongue is what defiles the whole body.” And when the body is defiled, the heart must also be corrupted along with it.
So Paul rightly said, “People whose hearts are corrupted.” These evil words corrupt good hearts.
Seek Paul as the blessed Thecla did, so that you may hear Paul's words.
You need wings. But if you have no wings, then [?] your feet to go up on high.
Let your eyes look downward, but let your heart be in the heights of heaven.
You need great vigilance, for your adversary stands against you, alert.
He threw him out of the paradise on earth. Now that he sees you going up to heaven, he will not neglect it.
Listen to the one who says, “I want you to be free from anxiety.”
Have no concern at all except concern for the kingdom of heaven alone.
If you desire to go up to heaven with the body that comes from the earth, tame the flesh through fasting and make it light, so that it may rise easily to the heights.
For when a horse eats too much, it cannot run, nor can it walk in an orderly way; instead, it behaves unruly. And if Israel had not eaten, it would not have kicked.
Lift your eyes to heaven, where the one you love is, and overcome the passions through holy love.
Prayer and faith will help you. Holy Scripture teaches you. Already here, you have a pledge of the places of rest in heaven.
You do not live with a woman who makes you stumble. You do not worry about children. You have been freed from the anxiety of raising children.
Follow your Lord, who leads you into the kingdom of heaven.
Follow the one who says to you, “If you walk toward me uprightly, I too will walk toward you uprightly.”
If you want to resemble Christ, follow his footsteps.
The gate is narrow and constricted. It is the righteous who enter through it.
Listen to the blessed Daniel saying, “I, Daniel, was mourning for three weeks.”
I have not eaten bread for pleasure, and meat and wine have not entered my mouth.
John, while living in the wilderness, did not acquire a vineyard for himself, so that he might make himself uncultivated.
You too, let these things be ready for you as instruction.
You have chosen for yourself a way of life directed toward heaven.
Fight the good fight of faith, looking ahead to the crown of righteousness.
Let your running be steadfast.
For it is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God.
Do you not see the images of kings, how some of them are large and beautifully adorned?
Others, however, have become blackened with time, have deteriorated, and have become objects of ridicule.
This is how all our deeds will be revealed in that place, like images.
Let us flee from that everlasting shame.
Let us too say, “Protect me, Lord, for I have trusted in you, because you have no need of my good things.”
Indeed, he needs nothing that belongs to you, except only the salvation of our souls.
Therefore let us offer ourselves as a living, holy sacrifice, as it is written. We will offer ourselves not through fire, but through patience and endurance.
For he said, “The one who endures to the end is the one who will be saved.”
And again, “He has labored forever; he will live to the end.”
Therefore, since we have chosen for ourselves a life without worry and without turmoil,
let us run well so that we may attain it, as it is written.
For it is no small danger to violate the commitment we made with the Lord.
Therefore, let us discipline our tongue and discipline our eyes, and lift up our hands in holiness, and train our feet to walk uprightly.
Acquire for yourself a good and blameless way of life, humility, and modesty.
Peace of mind; moderation in eating; strong self-control; love of hard work; sympathy; brotherly love; a spirit of fellowship; sound faith.
Although we speak of all these things in this way as if they were small matters, they require a great struggle for you to accomplish them.

He said, “The kingdom of heaven is like virgins.” He did not say that it is like the sun and the moon and the beautiful chorus of stars, or gold that will perish, or beauty that fades, or heaven itself.
See the dignity of purity: it is above everything.
This is what Paul, the bride’s escort, spoke about when he said, “But I want you to be free from worry.”
For this reason, we ought to pray that those who are healthy, namely the virgins, may continue in their health.
And that those who are sick, namely those who have fallen into sin, may receive healing.
We too ought to weep in this way and wash our eyes, which have looked with evil intent.
You have seen the wound, and you know the cure.
Secure the windows of your soul—not only your ears and your eyes and your mouth.
For these are the windows through which the evil one enters, as it is written: “Death has entered through your windows.”
Let the commandments of modesty govern your eyes and your ears.
Let psalms be in your mouth, along with meditation on the Scriptures.
Therefore, we ought to open our windows to God—that is, our senses—and close them against the enemy.

You too, say with that holy soul, “I will climb a palm tree and take hold of its high branches.” This means, “I will lift my thoughts up to heaven and hold firmly to an upright faith, so that I will not slip among earthly things.”
But take heed: the palm tree has thorns, which are the rebukes that pursue sin.
For he said, “The words of the wise are like goads for oxen and like nails firmly driven in,” so that, as these keep piercing your heart, you may keep yourself away from every sin.
But he said, “Take hold of its high branches,” so that you may be on high and be able to stand firm under the temptations that come upon you.
At the appropriate times, always read the holy Scriptures.
For just as wine, when drunk, soothes sorrow and turns the heart toward gladness, so the spiritual wine, which is the reading of the Scriptures, turns the soul toward joy.
Let the remembrance of God be in your heart at all times, as you too say with David, “I always saw the Lord before me, for he is at my right hand so that I will not be shaken.”
Let these words be written on your hand and fixed before your eyes.
If you honor God through his commandments, he will be at your right hand.
But if you dishonor him through your transgressions, the devil will be at your right hand.
For this is how Scripture testified about Judas when he became a transgressor: “Let the devil stand at his right hand.”
Give glory to God at all times, saying, “I will exalt you, my God, my King.”
Give him glory through deeds, not through words.
This is how David gives him glory, saying, “I will bless you forever and forever and ever”—not for just one day, or one month, or one year, but for his entire lifetime.
For he knows that when a person reaches perfection, then he begins in virtue.
But you will often say, “What kind of heart can give glory to God at all times?”
It is a heart like that of the blessed Paul, who writes, “I am not aware of anything I have done.”
And again, like David, who says, “Cleanse me, Lord, of my hidden faults.”
It is this kind of heart that the Savior commanded us to acquire for ourselves, saying, “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they will see God.”
This is what the person who does not sin against God is like.
This is the one who gives glory to God through his words and his deeds.
Such a person, even if illness, poverty, or death comes upon him, will not lose heart.
Rather, he too will say with Paul, “Who can separate us from the love of God?” and the things that follow these words.
Remember the day—that terrifying day, full of trembling [?].
At that time we will stand before the holy judgment seat to give an account of everything we have done, in the place where the sins we have committed will be set before everyone's eyes.
And they will be exposed before those who do not know about them.
In the place where the river of fire and the undying worm are.
At that time the books of our hearts will be opened, spread out, and read aloud in the midst of that assembly.
And all the deeds we have done will be revealed: the public ones and the hidden ones, those of the night and those of the day, those we have done carelessly and forgetfully;
those we have done with the members of the body, and those we have carried out through the movements of our heart.
At that time we will understand through experience and actual events that the things we do in secret will be exposed then.
Remember that we must depart from this place and go before the Judge who cannot be deceived.
He is the one who will uncover what is hidden in darkness and reveal the intentions of hearts, and examine our deeds, our thoughts, and our words.
At that time we will receive severe punishments for the sins we have committed, which we think are small.
Remember at all times, and do not forget any flame of Gehenna that never goes out.
Set the Judge before your eyes in advance—the one who is coming to judge the living and the dead.
Think of the thousands upon thousands and the tens of thousands upon tens of thousands of angels standing before the Judge at that time.
Let your ears hear in advance the sound of the trumpets and the terrifying voice of that Judge.
Let your eyes see beforehand the things that are destined to happen.
Some are thrown out into the outer darkness.
Others, after the struggle and hardship of virginity, have the door of the heavenly bridal chamber shut against them.
See some being bound like bundles and thrown into the fiery furnace.
Others have their hands and feet bound and are thrown out into the outer darkness.
Some are handed over to the sleepless worm and the gnashing of teeth.
One is being put to shame because he laughed improperly, at the wrong time.
Another, because he caused his brother to stumble, or because he oppressed his neighbor.
Another is judged for hidden sins that he committed.
Another has punishments decreed against him for idle words that he spoke.
Another is condemned for his evil intentions.
Another has the door of the kingdom shut against him because of insults he uttered.
Another has been handed over to punishment without relief because of his hatred of evil.
Another has been given over to disgrace and shame forever.
Others have been entirely deprived of the knowledge of God. They heard, “I do not know you or where you come from.”
Because they engaged in deeds that are hateful to Christ.

Since these things are so, what kind of people ought we to be, except to pour down torrents of tears every day and say, together with the prophet, “Who will give water to my head and a spring of tears to my eyes,
so that I may weep over my sins day and night?” This is so that we may be able to escape the punishment that is to come.
Let us first confess our sins before that dreadful place of judgment.
Let us appeal to the Lord’s mercies as long as we are in this dwelling place.
For he said, “Who will give you thanks in Hades?”
Let us understand this, my beloved: God gave us all the natural parts of our body in pairs.
Indeed, he gave us two eyes, two ears, two hands, and two feet.
If one of these becomes impaired through illness, we meet our need through the other.
But he gave us only one soul. If we destroy it through negligence, how will we live?
Let us therefore take care of it and put nothing above its salvation, because it is the soul that will be made to stand for judgment and give its defense before that judgment seat.
But if at that time you say before the judge, “It was money that deceived me,”
The judge will answer you, “Then did you not hear me calling out to you, ‘What will a person gain if he gains the whole world but loses his soul?’”
“Or what will a person give in exchange for his soul?”
He will also say to you, “Eve gained nothing when she said, ‘It was the serpent that deceived me.’”
Now then, brothers and sisters, with these things in our hearts,
come, let us stir up our own eagerness.
Come, let us give glory to God before darkness comes, before that great and manifest day comes upon us.
This is the day the prophet spoke about, saying, “Look, the Lord is coming!”
Who will be able to endure the day of his coming?
That day is terrifying. It is a day of darkness and gloom, a day of clouds and thick darkness, a day of shouting and trumpet blasts.
But perhaps you will say, “Who will be able to escape all these things?”
Listen, I will teach you.
For do not think that you will be able to escape merely by keeping your body pure.
Rather, when someone does you harm, do good to him in return.
When people slander you, respond with wisdom.
When people curse you, bless them in return.
When you fast, do not become proud. For true fasting is not merely abstaining from food; it is also abstaining from sins.
We ought to examine the Scriptures.
For notice that what the prophet first saw was a rod of walnut wood.
Afterward, it was a bronze cauldron with a fire burning beneath it. This reveals that whoever will not endure the rod of correction here will be tested by the fire of Gehenna in the other place.

In this very same way, Moses was shown a pillar of light and a pillar of fire, proclaiming to everyone, “Whoever obeys the law will enjoy the sweet, true light. Whoever disobeys will be handed over to the fire.”
Read the Gospels, and you will understand that when we leave this world, no one will be able to help us.
No brother will be able to rescue a brother from the unending torments. No friend will be able to help his friend.
Nor will parents be able to help their children, or children their parents.
And why am I speaking merely about people like these?
For even Noah, Daniel, and Job will not be able to save a son or a daughter.
But you will often say to me, “What is the proof of these words?”
Look at this man who had no wedding garment on, when they threw him out of the wedding hall.
None of those who were reclining at the meal interceded for him.
Look also at the servant to whom they gave the talent, when they threw him into the outer darkness.
No one pleaded on his behalf.
Look also at the five virgins, when the door of the wedding hall was shut against them.
Their fellow virgins did not petition the bridegroom on behalf of those whom Christ called foolish.
For after they had trampled down the flame of pleasure and extinguished the heat of desire, after many fasts and nights of keeping watch, after sleeping on the ground,
then they were called foolish. And truly, they were justly called by this name, because they had accomplished the great task of virginity,
but they had forgotten the small and easy task of kindness to others.
Think of the judge as he places the sheep at his right hand and the fruitless goats at his left, saying to those at his right hand, “Come and inherit the kingdom.”
But as he throws those at his left hand out into the outer darkness, none of those at his right hand was able to help them.
What he said is true: “Here is the man and his work.”
Have you not heard about that rich man who made a plea to Lazarus because he longed for a drop of water while he was being burned in the place of torment?
You see that Abraham could not save him from the place of torment, even though he begged him.
Therefore, let us help ourselves while we are still here, and give glory to God before darkness comes—that is, before we are banished into the darkness.
It is better for our tongues to become dry here through fasting than for us to long for a drop of water in the other place and not be given any.
Let us strive to escape great torments through small hardships here.

Remember that if a fever comes upon us for a few days, and if we see those being punished by the judges of this world, trembling and distress seize us, even though the punishment and the place of judgment here last only a short time.
What, then, must the punishment in the coming place of judgment be like, the punishment in which we will be punished for endless ages?
Therefore, let us hurry to enter through the narrow gate, and let us not walk through the wide one, knowing that all the affairs of this world are like dreams, and all are destined for destruction.
For illness destroys the strength of the body, and beauty fades through old age.
And even if we enjoy a lavish table, when evening comes we forget its pleasure.
In short, everything here is like these cobwebs and dreams.
Therefore, the Savior rightly called those who suffer affliction blessed, because the pleasures of this world cannot overpower them.
Therefore, just as Abraham heard, “Come out of your land,” let us too come out of our lawless deeds.
And let us pray with holy David, saying before God, “I have praised you seven times a day for your righteous judgments.”
For it is a good thing to speak with God at all times through prayer.
For if the company of a good person changes anyone who associates with him for the better, how much more someone who speaks with God night and day through prayer!
Who would ever sin while thinking that God is beside him?
So let us remember the one who said, “Pray at all times,” so that sin may not find a way into our hearts through forgetfulness.
Reflect on death beforehand, and put to death your members that are on earth. The day of the Lord is coming like a thief.
When those who will take your soul come for you, will you say, “Be patient with me, so that I may fast, show mercy, and repent”?
They will say to you, “Have you not heard the Lord crying out, ‘The kingdom of heaven has drawn near’?”
Then have you not heard him saying, “Show mercy, so that mercy may be shown to you”?
Then have you not heard Paul saying, “As long as we have time, let us do what is good”?
Anyone who wants to be saved does not need long periods of time.
For did the thief need long periods of time? He only believed, and he gained paradise.
And the holy martyrs inherited the kingdom of heaven in a short time.
They gave their blood; you, in turn, give your tears.
The one who said, “I want everyone to be saved,” does not lie. That is why he not only teaches us through the holy Scripture, but also teaches us through the misfortunes and sufferings of others.
For we see physicians cutting into people, and rulers sitting on the judgment seat punishing thieves, so that through the sufferings of others we may become instructed.
Now then, my beloved, since we have taken root in faith, let us run onward to knowledge, and from knowledge into love, and from love to the inheritance in heaven.
Let [?] persevere in prayer, as it is written.
Shepherds, even when there is no wolf near them, keep watch through the night over their flock of sheep. Even when there is no wild beast, their dogs keep watch beside them.
That is why it is good to watch our conduct at all times, even when no temptation is upon us. Still, the exercise will not harm you at all; rather, you will gain all the more.
For who could fail to benefit from keeping watch through the night in prayer?
Therefore we must be watchful in every direction, lest evil dwell in our soul.
For if a soul falls into the clutches of sin and persists in insensibility, it greatly aggravates the sickness of sin.
For just as a spark of fire, if it catches in some wood, burns it on every side,
so too is the nature of sin: if it succeeds in ruling the soul’s thoughts, it destroys the whole soul, and the body along with it.
That is why we must repel the beginning of sin, turning it back like an unruly horse.
If we will have to give an account for an idle word, how much more for the sins that lead to death!
Do not let the sweetness of the affairs of this life deceive us.
For human affairs are no different from dreams and shadows, and they pass away like [?] flowing water.
Do not marvel at possessions and wealth, but look at how they pass from one person to another, and from this other [?] to yet another.
Therefore, it is right to despise them.
For the written saying is very fitting: “The things we see are temporary, but the things we do not see are eternal.”
Those things do not diminish and cannot perish. They are not subject to change.
Let us therefore make every effort to acquire these things for ourselves.
Let us struggle for these things, for we cannot acquire any of them for ourselves once we have departed from this life.
For athletes do not receive a crown if they abandon the contest. Therefore, let us seize the crown for ourselves and escape shame and loss.
For he said, “The person whose work is burned up will suffer loss.”
Then what kind of fire is this [?] for us?
Then what kind of darkness is the outer darkness?
Then what kind of place is the place of weeping and gnashing of teeth?
Take these things to heart, and keep your soul a virgin until the bridegroom comes in his glory.
You too should sing psalms, saying, “My soul is always in my hands, and I have not forgotten your law.”
And say, “You are the one who will save me from the hunters’ trap.”
Let your lamp remain burning. Do not let them find you inattentive.
Even if sleep is sweet to you at night, know that nothing is sweeter than the psalms.
For the holy one said, “Your words have become sweeter in my throat than honey in my mouth.”
The martyrs give their own lives for the name of God.
Let us, for our part, offer our practice of self-denial.
Remember that burning coals were spread beneath the martyrs.
You, for your part, should not consider it difficult to sleep on the ground.
If your mouth becomes foul and bitter from fasting, remember that the one who made the sweetness of honey tasted bitterness for your sake.
Even if you have wept once over your sins, you have not yet become like Paul, who wept over the salvation of others.
Let us therefore encourage one another with these words. The suffering lasts only a short time, but the rest is eternal.
Overcome suffering through hope.
For he said, “Suffering produces endurance, and endurance produces hope, and hope does not bring shame.”
Consider that pleasure lasts only for a moment, but punishment lasts forever.
Reject the sweetness of pleasure because of the anguish of punishment.
Do not let the devil use our bodily members like arrows. Guard yourself; do not let him pierce you with the arrow of the belly’s craving.
For you know that after the people crossed the sea, they did not drown. Yet [?] on land through the belly’s craving.
Look at the suffering of those people and flee from their downfall.
If God did not spare your people—that is, those people back then—he will not spare you either if you are negligent.
But if you struggle with all your heart, with sound faith, you will rejoice with everlasting joy and gladness.

Therefore, pay attention at all times to these teachings, which are full of salvation. Keep them and carry them out, so that the Holy Trinity may be glorified in you: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, now and always, forever and ever. Amen.
Apa John, archbishop.
